Sunday night futures are trying to repair Friday's damage: ES 7640.0 (+0.34%), NQ +0.68% and Dow futures +0.29%. That follows a heavy cash session on Fri Oct 30: S&P 500 7580.07 (-1.82%), Nasdaq Composite 25437.0 (-2.86%), Russell 2000 -1.66%, with US Info Tech -4.24% on the day and VIX up 12.9% to 19.42. The biggest story is still low-quality credit. On the Bloomberg HY ladder, the Caa-B gap is 781bp, at the 99.6th percentile of its 5-year range (5y average ~416bp), up 103bp in a month and 242bp in three months. Caa OAS is 1116bp, the widest since April 2020. The open question is whether that CCC stress is spreading. So far it is spreading only partly: single-B widened 25bp in a month to 335bp, but Ba is up only 9bp to 204bp and IG is 90bp (+7bp, 1m). The 63-day Caa/B correlation rose to 0.65 from 0.47 a month ago and 0.41 three months ago, though it is still below its 0.69 5-year median. Read that as contagion pressure building at the bottom of the junk ladder, not yet a break into higher grades. This is descriptive, not a validated signal. The tech-phase model still places the tech basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm): basket drawdown -15.1%, 18 days after the Oct 6 peak. One signpost has triggered: 57.1% of basket names are more than 20% off their highs, against a 50% threshold. The model's odds of ever reaching Phase 2 or worse are 0.347 at 3 months and 0.412 at 6 months; these are model estimates. The relief-rally watch is not armed. AI-credit backstop gauges are quieter: CoreWeave 5Y CDS is ~1036bp, 158bp below its Oct 15 record, and Nvidia CDS rose only 5.4bp, so the market is not yet testing Nvidia's backstop. Sentiment versus the prior session has moved from forced de-risking to a tentative, futures-led stabilisation. Defensives, gold (+0.91% tonight) and energy keep the leadership, and Brent at 111.21 is still well above $100 even after falling ~2% tonight.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

Widening velocity, not level. Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. ARMED marks elevated tail RISK, not a sell: 78% of past ARMED episodes did not produce a 10% drawdown. This rule failed all three pre-registered gates as a tradable overlay (placebo p=0.465); do not size positions off it. See the monitor_spread skill (MONITOR_SPREAD.md).

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.49 vol points (11th percentile of the 57 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 100.2 (72th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 84bp (flatter by 12bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (123bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 31 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 60/100 — Persistent, not accelerating. The core-trend measures (median, trimmed-mean and sticky) all sit near the middle-to-upper part of their history and are mostly flat, with only Median CPI drifting lower. That points to embedded inflation around 2.6-2.8%, not a re-acceleration. Core PCE at 3.12% is above that cluster, so the Fed's preferred gauge is the outlier on the hot side. The risk is breadth and the volatile components. Flexible CPI is 6.12% and rising (z 0.76, 82nd percentile), consistent with energy at $100+ oil. The Dallas Fed distribution shows a large share of the PCE basket rising at 3% or faster (16.6% of items above 10%, 10.2% at 5-10%, 25.8% at 3-5%), against 25.6% falling. Wage pressure is not the driver: AHE 3.0%, ECI 0.8. With 1y breakevens at 2.61% above 5y at 2.47%, the market sees this as a near-term energy-driven bulge rather than a de-anchoring. That supports a hawkish-hold-to-hike Fed bias, not cuts.

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
9 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 59/100
Today is far less extreme than March 2000 on froth, but further along on the catalyst and regime gauges than the price action suggests. On Equity Froth (computed), Nasdaq trailing P/E is 39.62x, only 15% of the way to the 2000 peak's 175x. Its stretch above the 200-day is 3% of the way, and SOX P/E 36.66x is 42% of the way. On Late-cycle Catalyst, credit is tighter than in 2000 (IG at 125% and Baa-10Y at 157% of the peak tightness condition), the curve is 67% of the way, and PMIs have not rolled over (9-10%). On Macro Regime, commodities-vs-equities reads 200% and the dollar 40%. On Bear-Market Signposts, VIX complacency is 154% and NFCI 152%, while AAII (40%), consumer confidence (31%) and margin debt (40%) are subdued. The tech-phase model puts the basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm): basket -15.1% versus -19.5% for the 2000 basket at the same day count. The model gives 0.535 odds of still being in Phase 1 at 6 months, 0.347 and 0.412 odds of ever reaching Phase 2 or worse at 3 and 6 months, and 0.402 odds of Phase 4 (trough/healing) at 12 months. These are model estimates, not certainties. The breadth signpost has triggered (57.1% of names more than 20% off their highs), and SOX is -27.0% from its 52w high, close to the -30% signpost.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (40x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analogy fits the shape of this selloff, with leadership cracking first and indices lagging, but not the valuation extreme. Nasdaq multiples are roughly a quarter of 2000's, and the market is pricing an earnings-backed AI cycle rather than eyeball metrics. The more worrying parallels are on the credit side: very tight IG and Baa spreads (complacency), loose financial conditions and a low-quality junk market that is already cracking. In 2000-01 the equity bust turned into a credit and economic event once spreads moved from the bottom tier into the middle. That is the hinge today. Phase 2 in the model needs HY OAS around 420-448bp and Baa-10Y around 195bp; those levels are 80-108bp and 41bp away. Concentration, CAPE and market-cap/GDP (analyst estimates, not verified by search this run) are at or near record territory, so the cushion if earnings disappoint is thin. The model's historical phase-conditional tilt favoured gold, Treasury duration and IG credit over mega-cap growth.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Hawkish hold, with a live risk of a 25bp hike at the next FOMC (analyst inference). In his Aug 28, 2026 Jackson Hole speech, Warsh said inflation is still too high, is unlikely to return to target on its own, and may require rate increases in the coming months. He also said inflation data are more concerning than the labor market. Today's inputs fit that view: core PCE 3.12%, flexible CPI rising, unemployment 4.2% and initial claims 194k. I could not verify what the Fed did at its September or October meetings, so the current policy rate is flagged as unverified. Coverage at the time cited roughly 3.6%.

~1 YEAR

Over roughly a year, policy is likely to be held at or above current levels, with one or two hikes possible if core PCE stays above 3% (inferred). Cuts are only likely if credit stress, now visible in CCC spreads, spreads into the real economy. Warsh's skepticism about forward guidance points to less telegraphing and more meeting-by-meeting surprises. His long-held view favouring a smaller Fed balance sheet suggests continued balance-sheet restraint (inferred from prior on-record positions, not verified this run).

At Jackson Hole Warsh gave his clearest hawkish signal yet, while stopping short of committing to a hike. Market odds of a September hike jumped afterwards; reports cited figures from a coin flip to 57% on CME FedWatch. He argued that forward guidance should be limited and circumscribed in normal times. Reporting also notes the President has defended Warsh while criticizing other officials who favour higher rates, a political cross-current to watch around the Nov 3 midterms. The near-term and one-year calls above are inferences from these statements, not announced policy.

Sources: AP via Local10 — Fed Chair Warsh signals rate hikes may be needed with US inflation stubbornly elevated (Aug 28, 2026) · Odds of higher interest rates soar after Fed Chair Warsh's remarks · PBS NewsHour — Fed Chair Warsh speaks at Jackson Hole
